results.title: Retrain a predictive model in ITSI | Splunk Docs
results.content: # Retrain a predictive model in ITSI. It is good practice to continuously monitor your incoming data, including historical KPI and service health score values, and retrain a model on newer data if KPIs or entities are added, removed, or changed. For example, if you add an Oracle database to a service, it is best practice to retrain the service's model because the new architecture will create new KPI relationships. For a model to accurately predict health scores in IT Service Intelligence (ITSI), the data it's making predictions on must have a similar distribution as the data on which the model was trained. Because data distributions are expected to drift over time, deploying a model is not a one-time exercise, but a continuous process. ## When to retrain a model. If monitoring your services for changes is too time consuming, a simpler strategy is to train the model periodically. For example, to capture changes to KPIs or service architecture, you might retrain a model every 10 days. Retrain a service's model in the following situations:. Before you retrain a model, test it on recent data to evaluate whether it needs to be retrained. * To retrain a model, the model must be saved in the service definition. For more information, see Train a predictive model in ITSI. 1. Test the model on recent data:. 1. From the Predictive Analytics tab of the selected service, navigate to the Test a Model section. Changing the time period retests the model on a recent set of data to determine if it needs to be retrained. For example, if a new KPI was added yesterday, test the model on the last 24 hours. 4. Analyze the model's metrics. If the metric values have dropped to unacceptable levels for your business, consider retraining the model. 2. Retrain the model on new data:. The existing model is replaced by the retrained model. For information about evaluating models, see Test a predictive model in ITSI in this manual. 4. Click Save to save the retrained model into the service definition. The following diagram illustrates the workflow for retraining a model:. * When to retrain a model.

results.title: Data Drift in Machine Learning: How to Detect, Handle, and Retrain Models for Reliable Performance | by Akanshu Sonkar | Medium
results.content: # Data Drift in Machine Learning: How to Detect, Handle, and Retrain Models for Reliable Performance. Machine learning models are trained on historical data to make predictions — but the world doesn’t stand still. When the data your model sees in production no longer matches what it learned from, this is called **data drift**. Left unaddressed, data drift leads to poor predictions, business losses, and eroded trust in AI systems. ## What is Data Drift? **Data drift** — also called **covariate shift** — happens when input feature distributions in production diverge from training data, undermining model performance. > “Data drift is a shift in the distributions of the ML model input features.”. **Example:** A demand-forecasting model trained on in-store sales sees a surge of online orders — outside its training distribution — leading to poor predictions . ## Types of Drift. * *Univariate drift*: single feature shifts — easy to detect with tests on each feature. * *Multivariate drift*: joint distributions change even when marginals don’t — requires more advanced hooks (e.g., PCA-based). 2. **Concept Drift**: the relationship between inputs and outputs changes (e.g., fraud detection rules evolve). 3. **Prior Probability Shift**: the outcome class balance changes (e.g., higher churn rate over time). 4. **Training-Serving Skew**, **Prediction Drift**, **Data Quality Issues**: other forms of mismatch in pipelines. * Hidden drift can mislead without ground truth available. > “When ML models are in production… statistical properties change… leading to a decrease in accuracy.”. ## Detecting and Monitoring Drift. * **Evidently**, **NannyML**, **Azure ML Model Monitor** — integrate drift detection and alerting. ## When & How to Retrain. ### Retraining Triggers. * Statistically significant feature-level drift. * Periodic cadence (e.g., monthly) even with no drift. ### **Retraining Costs**. Balance frequency vs cost — e.g., only retrain when drift magnitude & impact justify it. ## Retraining Process. 3. **A/B test** with current and new model in production. 5. **Resume monitoring** the new model for any further drift. Data drift is inevitable in production ML. * **Monitoring** using statistical tests and targeted tooling. * **Strategic retraining** balancing performance vs cost. > “Detecting and addressing data drift is vital to maintaining ML model reliability in dynamic settings.”.

results.title: When to Retrain Your ML Models for Success - tech
results.content: Use the right retraining trigger—time-based, performance-based, or event-based—to keep machine learning models accurate, fresh, and cost-effective. "Retrain ML models when metrics or data shifts demand it—not just on a schedule—using performance and event triggers, with a light time-based backstop.". Event-based retraining might incur additional costs due to the need for sophisticated event detection mechanisms, though MLOps platforms are increasingly offering plug-and-play observability models to address this. Performance-based retraining ensures the model’s accuracy remains high by reacting to performance drops, while time-based retraining may frustratingly lag in adjusting to recent changes, potentially leaving you with an outdated model. Imagine a sudden global event or a new trending topic; your model needs to adapt instantly, and event-based retraining makes that possible by reacting to significant shifts in data or user behavior. For instance, a scheduled monthly retraining (time-based) augmented by performance-based triggers and event-driven retraining for significant shifts in data patterns can create a robust and adaptive system. machine learning  retrain models  model evaluation  model improvement  performance-based retraining.

results.title: 4.3. When to retrain machine learning models | Evidently AI - Open-source ML observability course
results.content: When to retrain machine learning models. When to retrain machine learning models, by Emeli Dral. ## Why retrain ML models? The good news is that new data is accumulated during model use. You can use this data to retrain and update your model. ## Model retraining strategies. **Pro-tip for scheduled retraining**: use historical data to determine the rate of model decay and the volume of new data required for effective retraining. For example, you can get a training set from your historical data and train a model on top of this dataset. Then, you can start experimenting: apply this model to new batches of data with a certain time step – daily, weekly, monthly – to measure how the model performs on the new data and define when its quality starts to degrade. * Will more data improve model quality? * How much data is needed to retrain the model? **Trigger-based retraining** To use this strategy, you need to pick a key metric – e.g., daily accuracy – and retrain the model if this metric breaks a certain threshold. For example, the retraining trigger may be “retrain the model if daily accuracy drops under 0.9.”. * Allows retraining the model automatically. ## Model retraining tradeoffs. The model retraining process isn't just about updating the model. Here are some considerations when deciding whether to retrain the model or not:. Remember to **fix the data quality first** and then confirm if retraining is needed. If the data quality is OK, it can be the data shifts that cause model performance issues. If you detect data drift, consider both **retraining** and **switching to alternatives** – rule-based systems, other models, or manual processes. Sometimes, you may have sufficient data to detect drift but not enough to retrain the model. It is useful to come up with a heuristic to define the minimum volume of data you need to retrain the model. We discussed two main strategies for model retraining: scheduled retraining and trigger-based retraining. * Monitor the production model quality and data. * Test your retraining strategy on historical data to make informed choices.
